source.title: How Small Can 6G Reason? Scaling Tiny-to-Small Language Models for AI-Native Networks
source.authors: M. Ferrag; Abderrahmane Lakas; Mérouane Debbah

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures downstream task accuracy across model parameter scales, a different measure and setting from the original held-out cross-entropy scaling studies. It tests downstream performance scaling, not pretraining loss scaling or compute-optimal training allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. in related work but reports no new held-out cross-entropy measurements, training-token or compute sweep, compute-optimal allocation, or controlled architecture comparison. Its own relevant results are zero-shot 6G-Bench accuracy across model sizes and group-level accuracy at the smallest and largest evaluated models.
record.test_reason: The study's own results show zero-shot downstream accuracy on a new domain benchmark (6G-Bench) across off-the-shelf instruction-tuned models from 135M to 7B, with a log-linear fit of accuracy against parameter count. This bears on V6 in a new setting. It does not measure pretraining loss, train models, or vary compute or data, so V1–V5 and V7 are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly right: a 1–1.5B transition, diminishing returns beyond 3B, architecture-dependent deviations, and 1.5–3B as the best balance of reliability and cost. Two additions: the authors also conclude that intent and distributed-intelligence tasks are most scale-sensitive while trust and resource management saturate earlier, and that the instability gap shrinks from 0.365 to 0.031. They call the transition an empirical phenomenon, not a theoretical phase boundary.
record.recipe_differences: The paper evaluates zero-shot, instruction-tuned models on 6G-Bench multiple-choice decisions and fits downstream accuracy against parameter count. It does not train language models under controlled data or compute budgets, nor measure held-out cross-entropy loss.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports architecture- and training/alignment-related deviations across the evaluated checkpoints, but does not isolate their causal effects. It uses one prompting protocol and reports no prompt sensitivity sweep.

fits_no_version.finding: The instability gap Δ5 = pass@5 − pass@1 contracts from 0.365 at 135M to 0.031 at 7B, measured on 7 tasks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Consistency between greedy and sampled answers improves with model scale.

fits_no_version.finding: Edge Score (accuracy per latency × VRAM) is non-monotonic in parameter count. LFM2-350M scores highest.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Deployment efficiency per unit of resource does not scale with parameter count.

record.problems: The measured outcome is downstream benchmark accuracy rather than held-out pretraining loss. The model sweep is heterogeneous in architecture, training data, and alignment, so parameter count is not isolated. The study uses one benchmark and one prompting protocol; the authors note the benchmark's bounded coverage and possible benchmark-author bias. The text gives 95% confidence intervals for pass@1 but not for the fitted coefficients. The stated scaling equation uses log(1+N), while the Table IV note describes residuals using log N.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports pass@3, pass@5, and the instability gap Δ5 in Table IV, as well as intermediate capability-group accuracy curves in Figures 2–6. These were not extracted as separate rows because the cataloged V6 evidence here focuses on the paper's primary deterministic pass@1 scaling result and the explicitly tabulated group endpoint comparisons; the stochastic metrics concern sampling robustness, and the plotted intermediate group series are not required to assess the primary trend. Inference-cost profiles and Edge Score results in Table VI and Figure 7 were also omitted because they measure deployment efficiency rather than downstream performance scaling.

untested.parts: Predictability from pretraining loss. Prediction or extrapolation of larger-model accuracy from smaller ones. Scaling under a common training recipe; models differ in data, architecture and alignment. Scaling beyond 7B. Other benchmarks or prompting protocols.
All: no pretraining loss is measured.
All: no controlled shape variation at fixed parameter count with loss measured.
All: no other modality or training-regime law.
All: no sensitivity of loss exponents to setup or fitting choices.

missing.what: Actual parameter counts differ from the nominal ones used in the fit (Llama-3.2-1B 1.236B, Granite-1B 1.462B, Olmo 7.298B, Qwen-7B 7.616B). The rows record only nominal sizes.
Intermediate per-model group accuracies, e.g. G1 Llama-1B 0.438 and G4 Llama-1B 0.321. These show non-monotonic within-group scaling. rows_left_out mentions the figures but does not extract them.

record.verdict_notes: The 1→1.5B jump (z≈13.9) compares Llama-1B with Qwen-1.5B, which are different families. Granite-1B already reaches 0.559 at nominal 1B, so the 'transition' is confounded with model family. The sweep is not controlled for data or recipe. Table III lists 11 models up to 8.34B, but LFM2-8B is used only for profiling. Not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining cross-entropy loss is measured against parameters, tokens, or compute.
No power law fitted to small training runs is used to predict the loss of larger runs.
No fixed-compute training sweep or loss-minimising parameter/token allocation is measured.
The study does not hold parameter count and training setup fixed while varying architecture to measure pretraining loss.
No other modality, repeated-data regime, fine-tuning scaling law, or transfer scaling law is tested.

Tests zero-shot accuracy on one 6G decision benchmark across model sizes. It does not test whether downstream performance is predictable from pretraining loss, other downstream tasks, or models trained under a controlled common recipe.

The paper reports architecture-dependent deviations in downstream accuracy, but does not test the sensitivity of cross-entropy exponents or compute-optimal allocations to fitting choices, nor whether cross-entropy loss curves bend away from a power law.

rows.subject: All evaluated models (OLS fit)

rows.note: The paper defines A(N)=α log(1+N)+β+ϵ(N), but the Table IV note describes residuals using α log N+β.
rows.check: This is the fitted coefficient, not a measured rate. The Table IV residuals are consistent with α log N + β (e.g. Llama -0.105), not the log(1+N) form in Eq. 4. No CI or fit-quality statistic is given. Nominal, not actual, parameter counts are used.

relationships.condition: Overall pass@1 on 6G-Bench across heterogeneous instruction-tuned models, 135M–7B
relationships.reason: Accuracy rises from 0.224 to 0.707, with a positive log-linear fit (α=0.115). Most residuals are small, and all five capability groups improve end to end (R1–R3, R5–R8, R10–R16).
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy increased from 0.224 to 0.707 with a positive log-linear slope α=0.115, mostly small residuals and end-to-end gains across all five capability groups.

relationships.condition: Models of similar size from different families or recipes
relationships.reason: Same-size models differ sharply: Granite-1B 0.559 vs Llama-1B 0.373, and Olmo-7B 0.652 vs Qwen-7B 0.707. Residuals reach -0.105/+0.081, so parameter count alone predicts accuracy only loosely (R4, R5, R9, R10, R11).
relationships.display_finding: Granite-1B scored 0.559 versus Llama-1B's 0.373, and Olmo-7B scored 0.652 versus Qwen-7B's 0.707, with prediction residuals reaching −0.105 and +0.081.

relationships.reason: Scaling sensitivity varies by domain, from 0.104 (G3) to 0.154 (G1), so the rate of gain is task-dependent (R12–R16).
relationships.display_finding: Scaling sensitivity ranged from 0.104 to 0.154 across capability groups, indicating different rates of improvement.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Overall deterministic 6G-Bench accuracy across the evaluated 135M–7B model range
reader_labels.reason: The reported accuracy rises from 0.224 at 135M to 0.707 at 7B, and the study fits a positive log-linear accuracy trend; see R1–R11.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports non-uniform gains and architecture-dependent residuals, including substantial accuracy differences between models at similar parameter counts; group sensitivities also differ from 0.104 to 0.154. See R2–R10 and R12–R16.
